@@34075234 <p> It 's been years since developers found that Nvidia 's main product , the GPU , was useful not just for rendering video games but also for high-performance computing of the kind used in 3D modelling , weather forecasting , or the training of AI models -- and it 's on enterprise applications such as those that CEO Jensen Huang will focus his attention at the company 's GTC 2022 conference . <p> Nvidia is hoping to make it easier for CIOs building digital twins and machine learning models to secure enterprise computing , and even to speed the adoption of quantum computing with a range of new hardware and software . <p> Seeing double <p> Digital twins , numerical models that reflect changes in real-world objects useful in design , manufacturing , and service creation , vary in their level of detail . <p> For some applications , a simple database may suffice to record a product 's service history -- when it was made , who it shipped to , what modifications have been applied -- while others require a full-on 3D model incorporating real-time sensor data that can be used , for example , to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ It 's at the high end of that range that Nvidia plays . <p> At GTC 2022 , the company announced new tools for building digital twins for scientific and engineering applications . Two groups of researchers are already using Nvidia 's Modulus AI framework for developing physics machine learning models and its Omniverse 3D virtual world simulation platform to forecast the weather with greater confidence and speed , and to optimise the design of wind farms . <p> Engineers at Siemens Gamesa Renewable Energy are using the Modulus-Omniverse combination to model the placement of wind turbines in relation to one another to maximise power generation and reduce the effects of the turbulence generated by a turbine on its neighbours . <p> While the Siemens-Gamesa model looks at the effects of wind on a zone a few kilometres across , the ambitions of researchers working on FourCastNet are much greater . <p> FourCastNet ( named for the Fourier neural operators used in its calculations ) is a weather forecasting tool trained on 10 terabytes of data . It emulates and predicts extreme weather events such as hurricanes or atmospheric rivers @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to Sydney , Australia , in early March . Nvidia claims it can do so up to 45,000 times faster than traditional numerical prediction models . <p> The system is a first step towards delivering a still more ambitious project that Nvidia calls Earth-2 . It announced in November 2021 that it plans to build a supercomputer using its own chips and use it to create a digital twin of the Earth at 1-meter resolution in its Omniverse software to model the effects of climate change . <p> To help other enterprises build and maintain their own digital twins , later this year Nvidia will offer OVX computing systems running its Omniverse software on racks loaded with its GPUs , storage , and high-speed switch fabric . <p> Nvidia is also introducing Omniverse Cloud to allow creators , designers , and developers to collaborate on 3D designs without needing access to dedicated high-performance computing power of their own , a way for CIOs to temporarily expand their use of the technology without major capital investment . <p> And it 's teaming up with robotics makers and data providers to increase @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ their digital twins better reflect and interact with the real world . <p> It 's already working with retailers Kroger and Lowes , which are using Omniverse to simulate their stores and the logistics chains that supply them . <p> Accelerated learning <p> Machine learning models can be computationally intensive to run , but are even more so to train , as the process requires a system that can crunch through complex calculations on large volumes of data . At GTC2022 , Nvidia is introducing a new GPU architecture , Hopper , designed to speed up such tasks , and showing off the first chip based on it , the H100 . <p> Nvidia said the chip will make it possible to run large language models and recommender systems , increasingly common in enterprise applications , in real time , and includes new instructions that can speed up route optimisation and genomics applications . <p> The ability to segment the GPU into multiple instances -- much like virtual machines in a CPU -- will also make it useful for running several smaller applications , on premises or in the cloud @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ requires less mathematical precision , but greater data throughput , and the H100 's design allows applications to trade one off against the other . The result , says Nvidia , is that systems built with the H100 will be able to train models nine times faster than those using its predecessor , the A100 . <p> Secure computing <p> Nvidia 's said its new H100 chips will also enable it to extend confidential computing capabilities to the GPU , a feature hitherto only available on CPUs . Confidential computing enables enterprises to safely process health or financial data in the secure enclave of a specially designed processor , decrypting it on arrival and encrypting the results before they are sent to storage . <p> The option to securely process such data on a GPU , even in a public cloud or a colocation facility , could enable enterprises to speed up the development and use of machine learning models without scaling up capital spending . <p> When that day comes , Nvidia 's sales to the supercomputing market may take a hit , but in the meantime its chips @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ quantum computing systems <p> Researchers at the intersection of quantum and classical computing have created a low-level machine language called the Quantum Intermediate Representation . @@34077101 <h> Antarctic ice shelf collapses after unprecedented heatwave <p> Some time on or around March 15 , an ice shelf called Conger that was the size of the city of Rome collapsed into the dark and not quite frigid waters off the east coast of Antarctica . <p> " The Conger ice shelf was there and then suddenly it was gone , " Professor Andrew Mackintosh , head of the School of Earth , Atmosphere and Environment at Monash University told the US news site CNET of the disappearance of the 1200 square kilometre expanse of ice . <p> US NATIONAL ICE CENTRE <p> The US National Ice Centre has confirmed that iceberg C-38 has calved from the Conger Ice Shelf in the Wilkes Land Region of Antarctica . <p> In the days since , scientists have been debating what the implications of the collapse might be . <p> Ice shelves are forced into the waters off the Antarctic by slow-moving streams of ice that flow off the continent into the ocean , where they can expand hundreds of metres beneath the ocean 's surface , CSIRO oceanographer Dr Beatriz Pena-Molino said . <p> The process can take thousands @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ rim of the continent , the shelves hold back the glaciers behind them , slowing the process of sea-level rise caused by climate change . <p> It is this attribute that has attracted so much attention from scientists in the days since the collapse was first observed when scientists analysed satellite images on Friday last week . <p> DR ROBERT ROHDE/@RAROHDE <p> Daily high temperature : Dome C , Antarctica . <p> Though ice sheets have collapsed in west Antarctica in recent years , such as the Larsen B , which disappeared into the ocean in 2002 after a series of warm summers , east Antarctica had been considered a lot more stable . <p> And this matters because east Antarctica holds much more water than the west . <p> Pena-Molino said : " If you were to melt all east Antarctica , the contribution to sea level rise is something like 55 metres . If you were to melt all of west Antarctica , it is 3.2m . " <p> Before the Conger collapsed , fissures on its surface had been observed . <p> Dr Will Hobbs , a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Tasmania , said : " It could have just been a freak weather event . That happens . But if this starts happening regularly , it would be seriously terrifying. ? ? <p> Pena-Molino said atmospheric warming of the west was known to have accelerated the collapse of ice sheets : " What happens is that the surface begins to melt and it creates ponds , and these ponds sort of wedge themselves into the ice and create all these weak points . " <p> The weakened ice sheets could be more vulnerable to movement in the ocean , which increases when there is less sea ice to dampen the waves . The past six years have seen record low sea ice coverage . <p> At present , there is not enough data around the location of what was the Conger ice shelf to know if the ocean has warmed significantly . Satellites are employed to track the water temperatures off the coasts of Australia but much of the data in that section of Antarctica is drawn from tagged seals . <p> It is not expected that the collapse @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ glacier that fed it is not large enough . <p> But the collapse of Conger has returned attention to the Thwaites Glacier and the ice shelf it feeds . Thwaites , a behemoth of ice 125km across , has come to be known by some as the Doomsday Glacier . <p> In 2020 , a New Zealand ski field shut for a week . Why ? It was so warm , the rain-soaked snow was falling off the slopes . <p> In December 2021 , research was published predicting that the ice shelf holding it in place could collapse within the next five years , speeding up the collapse of the glacier , which could raise global water levels by 65 centimetres over the coming 85 years . <p> The sort of fissures once observed on Conger have already been recorded on Thwaites .

@@34084336 <h> Why did horses die out in North America ? <p> What drove horses to extinction in the Americas ? Did humans have a hand in their demise , or did climatic changes and altering vegetation trigger it ? <p> A definitive answer has eluded scientists , but improving techniques and the growing value of DNA analysis has painted a clearer picture of events surrounding their demise . <p> While climate change dominates headlines in the modern era , it loomed large in the lives of the many species that inhabited the Americas thousands of years before mankind began belching carbon dioxide into the atmosphere . <p> The end of the Pleistocene epoch -- the geological period roughly spanning 12,000 to 2.5 million years ago , coincided with a global cooling event and the extinction of many large mammals . Evidence suggests North America was hardest hit by extinctions . <p> This extinction event saw the demise of the horse in North America . It survived only because the Bering land bridge that once connected Alaska and Siberia had enabled animals to cross into Asia and spread west . <p> The end of the Pleistocene also saw the end @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , short-faced bears , sabre-toothed cats , stag-moose , woolly rhinos and giant ground sloths . <p> The story of the North American extinction of the horse would have been cut and dried had it not been for one major and complicating factor : the arrival of humans . <p> Humans , too , made use of the land bridge , but went the other way -- crossing from Asia into North America some 13,000 to 13,500 years ago . <p> Why could the continent that gave rise to the horse no longer provide a suitable home ? <p> *** <p> The Bering Strait is a storm-prone stretch of water that separates two continents . <p> When we talk of a land bridge we tend to conjure up images of a narrow strip of terrain . The Bering land bridge was no such modest affair . <p> Its fortunes -- and very existence -- ebbed and flowed with rising and falling ocean levels . During cooler periods in the earth 's past , glacial ice would build up , dropping sea levels to expose or expand the land bridge . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ saw the land bridge reach about twice the size of Texas , and scientists have even given it a name -- Beringia . <p> You could even consider the current state of affairs , with a body of water separating Siberia and Alaska , as unusual . The land bridge has actually been in place more often than not during the past two million years or more . <p> It has come and gone for far longer than that . It first developed at least 70 million years ago and was a dry land route for the movement of plants and animals , including dinosaurs . <p> When submerged , sea-dwelling life was able to move between the Pacific and Arctic Oceans . <p> The distribution and nature of much life on earth have been greatly influenced by this crucial land bridge . Its appearance and disappearance would also have had an influence on climate , with the closing of the land bridge affecting ocean currents . <p> The bridge enabled near-global distribution for some species . Mammals from as far away as Africa were able to spread north and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ horses instead went westward from the Americas , where their respective species had developed . <p> Horses originated in North America 35-56 million years ago . These terrier-sized mammals were adapted to forest life . Over millions of years , they increased in size and diversified . <p> Horses got larger in size and underwent other changes to their feet and teeth to adapt to changing environments . From five million to 24 million years ago , a number of horses occupied niches to which they had adapted , including grazing the spreading grasslands . <p> It was about four million years ago that the genus of all modern horses arose . As animals chew grass , the silica wears down their teeth . Therefore , animals with longer teeth live longer because their teeth do n't wear as fast , and they can continue to feed . <p> As grasslands expanded , the horses with long teeth lived longer because they were best adapted to eating grasses instead of leaves . @@34086308 <h> Time to warn others <p> As the rain falls over the sodden northeastern corner of the North Island , in the midst of the misery the bad weather has brought for thousands , there is still something to be grateful for . <p> Flooding and slips after hundreds of millimetres of rain in the past week have caused huge damage and major disruption around Gisborne and across the Tairawhiti region , leading to comparisons with the effects from ex-tropical Cyclone Bola in March 1988 . <p> While it may seem like a desperate attempt to find a flash of silver to line the edge of the rain clouds with , at least the heavy rain warnings from MetService for the region were timely and accurate . <p> Not that warnings actually stop extreme weather in its tracks . Would n't that be nice ? But when people have confidence in the forecasts , and have enough time to make sensible preparations , their safety can be better assured , and properties , farms , stock and livelihoods better protected . <p> We have to remember that severe weather is not limited to Aotearoa . Climate change is shifting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ phases , some more active and others more subdued . As a result , the distribution of extreme heat , dangerous drought and torrential rainfall is also changing , and afflicting all corners of the Earth . <p> However , unlike in First World nations , disaster-prone countries in especially Africa , the Caribbean and the Pacific , do not have the luxury of accurate weather forecasts , let alone targeted warnings of approaching extreme weather . <p> For these countries , which may be densely populated , impoverished and with barely adequate infrastructure , the impacts of wind and rain , drought and heat and raging fire , are way worse . <p> As the BBC reported this week , on average every day during the past 50 years there has been either a weather or climate or water-related disaster somewhere in the world . This is a five-fold increase in the number of these extreme events over that half century , fuelled by climate change . <p> The United Nations has now asked the World Meteorological Organisation ( WMO ) to come up with a way of disseminating @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ five years . <p> It says about one-third of the world 's population of 8 billion has no weather warning system , while 60% of Africa 's 1.4 billion people are unprotected . <p> The $US1.5 billion scheme , to be funded from organisations including the World Bank and the Green Climate Fund , will be a massive undertaking . <p> Not only will it be expensive to install the equipment which monitors the atmosphere and the technology which interprets the data , but also it will take time to train meteorological staff , to build up the weather expertise and experience necessary so the people of these countries can have confidence in their predictions . <p> UN Secretary-general Antonio Guterres is right to say it is unacceptable for people of Third World countries to bear the brunt of the changing climate . Unfortunately , many of those people live in low-lying areas by the coast and by rivers , and are extremely at risk . <p> As dire warnings continue to be sounded about rising temperatures this century , and governments around the world stay suspended in inertia , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ difference for billions of vulnerable people . <p> It 's easy to become disillusioned at the rate of progress in dealing with climate change . Sometimes it seems like the only glaciers left will be the ones our leaders appear to be frozen inside . <p> But we need to remember that significant action can be taken to mitigate , even reverse , human damage to our planet . <p> The dangers of the growing hole in the ozone layer above the Antarctic were made clear by scientists in the mid-1980s . After the adoption of the Montreal Protocol in 1987 , and the phasing out of chloroflurocarbons , the ozone hole has shrunk considerably and is no longer the threat it was just a few decades ago . <p> That protocol is probably the most successful piece of environmental protection law to date . <h> Comments <p> It 's not just our leaders that are the problem though is it ? The answer is data mining . <p> Cryptocurrencies and assets use blockchain technology . In essence , transactions are verified and recorded on a blockchain , a public digital ledger that contains information about all transactions . <p> Blockchain technology ensures the integrity of crypto transactions , but it does so by using huge amounts of electricity . Bitcoin 's annual electricity consumption is more than three times that of New Zealand . This is due to blockchain 's distributed nature and use of cryptography and complex processing , which require considerable computational power . <p> Verifying transactions , or mining , is so energy intensive it has caused concerns about the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ year , Kazakhstan cut off crypto miners because of the country 's energy crisis . <p> When the electricity used by crypto comes from fossil fuels , the connection to climate change becomes clearer . @@34092062 <h> New thinking needed on worm resistance <p> While the chemical solution for worm control has worked well over the decades , it does have its downsides . <p> Gordon Levet is a Northland sheep farmer and ram breeder who has spent a lifetime breeding sheep for worm resistance and facial eczema ( FE ) tolerance . He began breeding for worm resistance in 1987 , recognising that there was a genetic component to a sheep 's ability to tolerate worms and this has shaped his thinking on the issue ... <p> After 34 years of breeding for the worm resistant trait there have been no guidelines to follow . <p> So far as I know , no individual or scientific establishment has succeeded in breeding sheep that have a moderate to high resistance to worm challenges . <p> For me it has been a fascinating journey into the unknown with some unexpected and pleasing results . <p> My thinking has evolved with the study of the data from about 25,000 faecal samples taken for a laboratory to count worm eggs . We have taken two or three samplings each year , a month apart , over the peak @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ram lambs were never drenched . About 400 ram lambs by 10 sires were involved . This provided valuable information on how the progeny of each sire were performing under a high challenge . <p> In nature , the immune system of animals evolves to a level where it would control diseases , infection resulting from injury and internal parasites . The health issues of sheep and goats would have been minimal where they roamed in small groups over vast areas of mountainous , arid regions of southern Europe and Asia . Their immune system evolved to meet these low challenges . <p> And then man became involved , reprogramming domestic animals by selective breeding to produce increased volumes of quality food and fibre . In doing so , large mobs were grazed on confined areas creating the ideal environment for diseases and worms to profligate . <p> Scientists had two options for a solution . Reducing worms via drenching with chemicals or breeding for a stronger immune system to control the greater challenge . They chose the former option as it was more readily achievable . Selective breeding for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The chemical solution worked well over the past seven decades . However , it had a downside in two respects . The over-use of drenching decreases the effectiveness of each chemical used and super worms evolved able to resist all chemicals and combinations . <p> Another negative was that the most susceptible animals survived and were indistinguishable from their resistant sisters and entered the breeding flock . Ditto rams in ram breeding flocks . <p> The net result , a much more worm-susceptible flock having to face increased challenges from super worms . <p> Over my lifetime , the lethal Barbers ' Pole worm has become more of a problem in my area . Seventy years ago this worm was a problem in the late summer-autumn period , or the months of February until April . <p> However , this worm has now evolved to be a problem all the year . My Down breeds , adults and lambs , have to be drenched every six weeks otherwise there are losses . <p> Why has this happened ? Warmer winters have n't helped . It could be the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the natural result of the huge increase in worm populations due to our modern farming methods , where deviants occur , as is presently happening with Covid . Or more likely , a combination of factors , known or unknown . <p> The immune system is the key to breeding for worm resistance and I now believe it is quite different to all the other traits we breed for , be they production traits , physical , survival , breed type or behavioural . <p> All these we need to continually breed for , otherwise they will regress and eventually be lost . <p> On the other hand , the immune system in nature evolves to a level it can control disease and internal parasite challenges . It then fluctuates up or down , according to the normal environmental changes in challenge . It is a normal , natural process . <p> However , the huge increase of worm challenges with modern farming is way beyond the normal variation and the immune system fails . Sheep that have been bred to have a high degree of resistance will then fluctuate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the lower level . <p> At this point , there would be no point in continuing to breed for the worm resistant trait , as the immune system would stabilise at this higher level . <p> I have taken into account what had happened to sheep when they escaped from the early French settlers of Louisiana in the US several hundred years ago . These feral sheep adapted to the sub-tropical climate -- whereas the farmed Suffolk sheep are severely challenged by the Barbers ' Pole worm to the extent that unweaned lambs need to be drenched to keep them alive . The feral sheep are completely immune to all worm species and self-regulate according to challenge variations . <p> When worm resistance becomes more established in New Zealand , I believe the immune system will adjust to the level of worm challenge present in a specific region . In effect , the immune system would be much stronger in regions in the north and considerably less so in southern areas . <p> Much of what I have written are my opinions based on practical experience , but there are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ resistance is an increasing problem that will challenge sheep farming . <p> Climate change and particularly warmer winters will be favourable for the Barbers ' Pole worm to become more dominant in southern areas . This also applies to fungi that produce toxins and other health issues that have plagued sheep farmers in the north . <p> A new effective drench is unlikely to be produced for economic regions . <p> The good news is that when the genetic option is chosen to control worm challenges , it is permanent with no costs and a winner for consumers . <p> Whether your pastures are starting to open up due to insect pressure , hard grazing or dry conditions , undersowing into existing pasture is a cost-effective method , according to Agricom product development manager , Allister Moorhead.
